title: Hundreds Pack Diwali Food Hampers in Birmingham for Families in Need
excerpt: Diwali Basket Brigade volunteers packed hampers in Birmingham, London, Manchester and Leicester this weekend. Each £10 hamper carries food, toiletries and a handmade Diwali card.
body:
• Hundreds of volunteers packed Diwali food hampers in Birmingham this weekend as part of the Diwali Basket Brigade, the BBC reported, with packing events also held in London, Manchester and Leicester on October 31 and November 1.
  • Each hamper costs £10 and contains essential non-perishable food, toiletries such as toothpaste, and a handmade Diwali card.
  • The hampers go through partner food banks and charities to socially deprived and vulnerable households of all faiths and backgrounds.
  • To help: the Brigade's 2026 campaign accepts donations through its JustGiving page — £10 funds one hamper.

Hundreds of volunteers spent the weekend filling food hampers in Birmingham, part of a Diwali effort the BBC reported is aimed at bringing hope to vulnerable households facing rising food prices. The packing is organised by the Diwali Basket Brigade, a community initiative run by The Diwali Foundation, a UK registered charity established in 2018.

What goes in a hamper

Each hamper costs £10 and contains essential non-perishable food items, toiletries such as toothpaste, and a handmade Diwali card, according to the Brigade's 2026 campaign page. This year's packing took place on October 31 and November 1 at venues in Birmingham, London, Manchester and Leicester. The hampers are distributed by partner food banks and charities to families they nominate.

The Brigade says that since it began, it has provided almost 24,000 hampers — the equivalent, by its count, of 345,000 meals weighing almost 116 tonnes. Last year alone, 5,500 hampers were packed and distributed, taking the running total to 24,670 by the charity's campaign figures.

Why Diwali, and why everyone

The initiative is deliberately open beyond the Hindu community. The hampers go to "socially deprived, and vulnerable families from all faiths and backgrounds," the campaign page states, and the volunteer base reflects that. As founder and trustee Deepak Parekh puts it on the campaign page: "DBB is our small collective effort to support and spread the message of hope, happiness, and giving at Diwali."

The charity's own site carries the other end of the story: one recipient, a mother of four whose Universal Credit payment was still three days away during half term, said she cried with relief when told she had been selected for a hamper. With Diwali falling on November 8 this year, the Brigade's model — a festival of light marked by feeding strangers — is the diaspora's charitable calendar at its most practical.

How to help: Diwali Basket Brigade (run by The Diwali Foundation) funds each hamper from donations; you can donate through its official JustGiving campaign page, where £10 covers one hamper.
